claims.notes: THE TOWN'S COMMITTEE MEN, NAMED. The meeting called to the Eagle Hotel in the previous issue appoints a corresponding committee of four and the postmaster keeps its minutes. Every one of the five is already in this corpus in another capacity — Peck reports the paper's price current and keeps the store at La Salle and South Water, Collins is half of the law firm one door east of Brewster Hogan, Hogan signs the letter lists — which is the point worth recording: the same twenty or so men run the town's commerce, its post office and its politics, and a reconstruction that puts a name on a building is usually putting it on one of them. The column is interleaved with the news column beside it, so `lines_of_claim` names the resolution's own lines.

The column is badly cut and the lines are interleaved with a New York political column, so what survives is a fragment; it is kept because three claims in this month — the card, this report and the second-term notice of 21 February — give the Chicago Academy a working calendar for the winter of 1833-34, which is the only school year this corpus can date at all.

claims.notes: THE CHICAGO MAIL TIMETABLE, over the postmaster's name — four mails a week in and three days a week out, with departures at six and eight in the morning. EASTERN in on Wednesday and out Thursday 8 A.M.; WESTERN, NORTHERN and SOUTHERN all in on Tuesday, the first two out Thursday at 6 and the last out Saturday at 6. This is the most concrete piece of infrastructure the month yields after the bridge specification: it says the post office was open and transacting on fixed days, that Thursday morning was the town's busiest hour at it, and it gives the rhythm the letter lists were generated by. The heading line above 'arrives every Wednesda' is lost to the column edge and 'Eastern' is supplied from the parallel structure of the three lines below it, which name their own mails.

claims.notes: FRESH BUTTER IN FEBRUARY, and it dates something. This is new copy — datelined the day of the issue — where Cohen's other advertisement in the same paper is the standing winter-clothing block from November. So the store was taking in country produce in midwinter and turning it round the same week, which is a small but real piece of how the South Water street frontage worked: these are not warehouses waiting on navigation, they are shops with weekly stock. The quantity is cut at the column edge and is left unsupplied. The placement is carried over from the standing advertisement in this same issue, and the offset text quoted is that advertisement's, not this one's.

claims.notes: THE FIRM THIS MONTH'S BEST PLACEMENT IS COUNTED OFF. Brewster, Hogan & Co. advertise four separate times in every February issue — flour and hickory nuts, forwarding and commission, a dry goods assortment, and a demand for settlement of accounts — and never once say where they are. The address is recovered the other way round: Collins & Caton's law office is 'one door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co., South Water-street', so the store is on South Water street, and the placement recorded here is that inference and is labelled as such in its offset text. It is NOT a corner and it is not a lot; it is a named store on a named street, which is what the anchor is worth.

The name is the one this project meets everywhere else in the record — the Kinzie house on the north bank, Kinzie's Addition where Hiram Pearsons lost his square timber — and here he is advertising as a forwarding and commission merchant with six correspondents named in the 18 February printing of the same block. R. A. Kinzie, who keeps the store the Man Trap stands one door north of, advertises separately. Two Kinzies trading in one town, and neither gives a street.

claims.notes:
THE SECOND HALF OF THE 1 JANUARY 1834 CHICAGO LETTER LIST, H TO W, AND THIS IS THE PRINTING IT IS MINTED FROM — the other half is minted from 1834-02-04 page 4 column 2, and the rule is set out there in full: ONE LIST, ONE COHORT, minted once per half from the single printing that carries that half best, every other printing recorded as a reprint with its names unminted.

WHY THIS COLUMN. It is the only one of the six February and January printings that carries the run from H through P with initials intact — 'Levi Hills 2', 'D. S. Haight', 'J. H. Kinzie', 'J. C. Lacey', 'Chester Marshall 2', 'Lauretta Plympton', 'Julius Perrin 2', 'C. H. Pease' — where 1834-02-18's column 3 skips from 'A. M'Daniel' to 'Noah Phelps' and 1834-02-04's column 3 has lost every initial to the column edge, leaving bare surnames. Seventy-three names and the postmaster's signature are minted here.

RULING 1 IN FULL: this is Chicago's own post office, so a listed name mints a RESIDENT CANDIDATE flagged `letter_list_only` and the weaker evidence stays distinguishable from a man who advertises. Two of these names are not weak at all: J. H. Kinzie and Dr. H. Richey both trade in this same paper, so the flag retires for them the moment their advertisement claims compile beside this one, which is the mechanism doing exactly what it was built for.

WHAT IS STILL LOST. The printed list ran in two alphabetical sub-columns; the segmenter kept the left one and the right one survives only as line-end debris. Four rows are debris in this printing and are quoted and left unread. The row read 'Dr. H. Riche' is minted as Dr. H. Richey on the strength of 1834-02-18, which prints 'Thos. H. Richey' — the surname is corroborated and the given name is NOT, so the initial is what is minted.

Page 4 column 2 of this issue carries the A-to-H half woven line-for-line through a poem, and the segmenter has kept only the right-hand two or three characters of each name: 'Askina 2', 'has. Babcoco', 'TV. C. Cleavelan', 'Ber: Harkinen'. Every name in it is already minted from 1834-02-04, which carries the same half legibly. It is extracted rather than passed over because the corpus's rule is that an absence somebody looked for is evidence and an absence nobody looked for is a hole: this records that the half IS printed here, that it was read, and that it was refused as a witness on the stated ground that a name cut to two characters is not a name.

claims.notes: NONE OF THIS LAND IS IN CHICAGO, and that is the finding. Every tract David Carver offers is described by township and range in the military and district lands well south and west of Cook county, not by lot and block in the plat. He is the same man who, a fortnight later, opens a storage, commission and LUMBER business in the town and charters a schooner for the first two trips of the season (1834-02-25, claim c007). So the pattern is a Chicago merchant holding downstate land as an investment while trading here — which is a caution for any reading of this corpus that treats a name in the paper as a name on a lot.

claims.notes: STARR FOOT'S GROCERY, and the stock list is the useful part: spirits by the barrel, flour by the barrel, MACKINAC WHITE FISH by the barrel, dried apples by the bushel, table salt and tin ware. Everything but the apples came across the lake, which is the winter economy of this town in one advertisement — nothing is being landed between December and April, so a February store is selling what it laid in before the ice. The September 1834 read has the town board meeting in Starr Foot's house; his store gives no address in any February printing.
